1. The animation compares two illustrative borrowers, Leo and Tessa. Each has a bar for their loan's own interest rate, a house, and a stack of gold coins. The caption says the stack shows how far apart the 15-year and 30-year offers sit, so it appears to be comparing 15-year and 30-year mortgage rates. The source is labeled as the Freddie Mac weekly mortgage survey. The labels read "ILLUSTRATIVE" and "US only · history, not a forecast."

2. Mostly the on-screen text changes. The legend lines are added one at a time: "your bar = your loan's own rate", then "your stack = how far apart the 15-year and 30-year offers sit", then "a dollar in the house is hard to get back." The bars, houses and coin stacks look essentially the same in all six frames. The small figure beside Tessa's house shifts slightly. Leo's coin stack is short and Tessa's is tall. There is also a faint dashed box on the right that seems to be an empty placeholder.

3. The animation is mostly explaining how to read its chart. Leo's rate bar and coin stack are small, and Tessa's are larger. If the stack really shows the gap between the 15-year and 30-year rates, the gap is bigger for Tessa. The last caption adds that money put into the house is hard to get back out. The frames give no numbers, so I can't say what the bars or stacks are worth.

4. The frames give no explicit advice. A viewer might infer two things: the rate on your own loan matters when deciding between paying down the mortgage and investing, and extra money put into the house is illiquid. Nothing on screen says to pay extra or to invest, and the "history, not a forecast" label warns against reading it as a prediction.

5. Neither inference came from a stated recommendation. The rate-comparison and illiquidity points are on screen as captions ("your bar = your loan's own rate" and "a dollar in the house is hard to get back"). Turning them into guidance about extra payments or investing is my own conclusion.
